claim: Pro-inflammatory macrophage activation plays a prominent role in cardiovascular disease (CVD).
source: Pro-inflammatory macrophage activation plays a prominent role in a large number of disorders including cardiovascular disease (CVD) (Aikawa and Libby, 2004; Glass and Olefsky, 2012; Glass and Witztum, 2001; Gregor and Hotamisligil, 2011; Liang et al., 2007; Randolph, 2014; Ridker and Lüscher, 2014; Tabas, 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Established treatments for CVD such as statins do not completely eliminate cardiovascular risk.
source: Established treatments for CVD such as those dependent on the cholesterol lowering effect of statins do not completely eliminate cardiovascular risk (Aikawa and Libby, 2004; Aikawa et al., 2001; Libby, 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Alternative novel solutions are needed to tackle residual cardiovascular risk by targeting pro-inflammatory activation in CVD.
source: therefore alternative novel solutions are needed to tackle such residual risk by targeting pro-inflammatory activation in CVD (Ridker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Characterizing the mechanisms underlying macrophage activation is challenging due to functional heterogeneity and complex interplay between pro- and anti-inflammatory phenotypes.
source: Characterizing the mechanisms underlying macrophage activation itself proves to be a challenging task, given the functional heterogeneity of macrophages and the complex interplay between the pro- and anti-inflammatory phenotypes (Biswas and Mantovani, 2012; Gordon and Mantovani, 2011; Koltsova et al., 2013; Lawrence and Natoli, 2011; Ley et al., 2011; Moore et al., 2013; Murray et al., 2014; Swirski and Nahrendorf, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Macrophage activation follows a spectrum model defined by specific stimuli rather than a bipolar model of pro- and anti-inflammatory polarization.
source: Furthermore, it is increasingly recognized that macrophage activation has many distinct types and follows a spectrum model defined by specific stimuli rather than the bipolar model of pro- and anti-inflammatory polarization that once prevailed (Murray et al., 2014; Nahrendorf and Swirski, 2016; Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Complex human diseases such as CVD arise from the concerted effects of multiple genes and their products forming complex networks of interactions.
source: Complex human diseases such as CVD are seldom the result of a perturbation of a single gene but rather arise from the concerted effects of multiple genes and their products forming complex networks of interactions in cells, collectively embodied in the 'interactome' concept (Vidal et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Network medicine has emerged as an effective quantitative framework to address the complexity of human disease.
source: Network medicine has emerged as an effective quantitative framework to address the complexity of human disease (Barabási et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Disease determinants tend to be localized in the same region in the interactome and interact closely with each other, forming 'disease modules'.
source: Increasing evidence suggests that disease determinants tend to be localized in the same region in the interactome and interact closely with each other, leading to their organization into 'disease modules' (Barabási et al., 2011; Goh et al., 2007; Menche et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Functionally similar genes form 'functional modules' in the interactome.
source: The same principle is valid for functionally similar genes, which form 'functional modules' (Shih and Parthasarathy, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Interactomes are incomplete and biased toward highly studied proteins.
source: Despite these advances, one important factor hampering the effective molecular characterization of diseases is that interactomes, which are collections of multiple types of literature-curated physical protein-protein interactions (PPIs) with experimental evidence from high-throughput experiments and small-scale studies, are incomplete (Menche et al., 2015) and biased toward highly studied proteins such as disease-related proteins or targets of pre-existing drugs (Rolland et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Interactomes are context-independent and do not carry information specific to cell type, experimental condition or pathological state.
source: Most importantly, interactomes are context-independent, that is do not carry information specific to the cell type, experimental condition or pathological state but rather represent the sum of all observed interactions, which makes them inherently generic and limits their utility in diverse biological and experimental settings.
evidence: Based on the definition and nature of interactomes as described in the text

claim: High-resolution/accuracy mass spectrometry offers an opportunity to characterize the proteome of a specific cell state in a comprehensive way.
source: Owing to its unbiased nature and high information content, high-resolution/accuracy mass spectrometry (MS) offers an opportunity to characterize the proteome of a specific cell state in a comprehensive way (Mann et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The study used unbiased macrophage-derived proteomics measurements to enhance the literature-curated human interactome by adding cell type- and condition-specific information.
source: Here, we used unbiased macrophage-derived proteomics measurements to enhance the literature-curated human interactome by adding cell type- and condition-specific information to it, thereby helping address its context-independence as well as its incompleteness.
evidence: Description of the study's methodology

claim: The study used interferon-γ (IFNγ) as an example of major instigators of pro-inflammatory macrophage activation.
source: We thus used interferon-γ (IFNγ) as an example of major instigators of pro-inflammatory macrophage activation.
evidence: Description of the study's experimental design

claim: Edges derived from macrophage-specific proteomics contributed to the less characterized parts of the interactome.
source: Our results revealed that edges derived from macrophage-specific proteomics contributed to the less characterized parts of the interactome
evidence: Summary of study results

claim: Edges derived from macrophage-specific proteomics reflected the respective macrophage stimulation condition in terms of pathways and biological processes.
source: Our results revealed that edges derived from macrophage-specific proteomics contributed to the less characterized parts of the interactome, reflected the respective macrophage stimulation condition in terms of pathways and biological processes
evidence: Summary of study results

claim: Addition of co-abundance edges increased the prediction performance of CVD therapeutic targets.
source: Our results revealed that edges derived from macrophage-specific proteomics contributed to the less characterized parts of the interactome, reflected the respective macrophage stimulation condition in terms of pathways and biological processes, and increased the prediction performance of CVD therapeutic targets.
evidence: Summary of study results

claim: The prioritized candidates showed significant enrichment with immune system and cardiovascular disease related signatures.
source: The top-ranked candidates for regulators of macrophage activation, and hence potential CVD drug targets, also showed significant enrichment with immune system as well as cardiovascular disease related signatures.
evidence: Summary of study results

claim: GBP1 and WARS were identified as top candidate drivers of inflammation based on network topology, transcriptomics and proteomics.
source: Integrating the novel network topology with transcriptomics and proteomics revealed top candidate drivers of inflammation. In vitro loss-of-function experiments demonstrated the regulatory role of these proteins in pro-inflammatory signaling.
evidence: Summary of study results combining multiple data types

claim: In vitro loss-of-function experiments demonstrated that GBP1 and WARS regulate the expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokine CCL2.
source: In vitro loss-of-function experiments demonstrated the regulatory role of these proteins in pro-inflammatory signaling.
evidence: Summary of experimental validation results

claim: In vitro loss-of-function experiments demonstrated that GBP1 and WARS regulate phosphorylation of STAT1.
source: In vitro loss-of-function experiments demonstrated the regulatory role of these proteins in pro-inflammatory signaling.
evidence: Summary of experimental validation results

claim: Co-abundance networks were built for baseline control M(-), IFNγ stimulated M(IFNγ), and IL-4 stimulated M(IL-4) phenotypes of THP-1 cells.
source: For each condition, we built co-abundance networks to represent the relationships between proteins that show similar abundance patterns over time by constructing the correlation matrix, setting a correlation threshold and building the network based on the edges above this threshold (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, see Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1 for a summary of topological properties).
evidence: Description of methodology with reference to figures

claim: Co-abundance networks have several-fold higher edge densities than the PPI network as a whole.
source: While the co-abundance networks have several-fold higher edge densities than the PPI network as a whole (Supplementary file 1), their edge densities are comparable to the region of the PPI that hosts the proteins in the co-abundance networks (0.96%).
evidence: Comparison of network properties

claim: Co-abundance networks display broad degree distributions.
source: Mirroring well-known properties of PPI networks, the co-abundance networks display broad degree distributions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Network analysis with reference to figure

claim: Co-abundance networks have high average clustering coefficients.
source: Mirroring well-known properties of PPI networks, the co-abundance networks display broad degree distributions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and high average clustering coefficients (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Network analysis with reference to supplementary file

claim: Co-abundance networks have higher diameters and higher average shortest path lengths compared to the PPI network.
source: Despite these similar characteristics, in comparison with the PPI network, the co-abundance networks have higher diameters and higher average shortest path lengths, as well as higher average clustering coefficients, possibly due to similar protein expression patterns connecting local groups of proteins all at once (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Comparison of network properties

claim: Co-abundance networks are more locally clustered and not as compact compared to the PPI network.
source: Thus, co-abundance networks are more locally clustered and not as compact, compared to the PPI network, overall suggesting a complementary topology to the PPI network.
evidence: Inference from network property comparisons

claim: Each macrophage stimulation condition was denser in certain regions of the PPI network.
source: Overlaying the co-abundance networks on the PPI network, we found that each stimulation condition was denser in certain regions, and overall filled in the sparse parts of the PPI network, resulting in a combined interactome where each condition can be distinguished and their overlapping regions can be assessed (Figure 1B).
evidence: Visual analysis of network overlay with reference to figure

claim: Co-abundance edges showed significant enrichment for shared Gene Ontology (GO) terms.
source: Co-abundance edges showed significant enrichment for (i) shared Gene Ontology (GO) terms, (ii) the literature curated PPI network used throughout this study, and (iii) interactions between pairs of proteins belonging to a common protein complex, based on high-quality protein complex databases and curated co-complex association maps (Figure 1C).
evidence: Statistical enrichment analysis with reference to figure

claim: Co-abundance edges showed significant enrichment for the literature curated PPI network.
source: Co-abundance edges showed significant enrichment for (i) shared Gene Ontology (GO) terms, (ii) the literature curated PPI network used throughout this study, and (iii) interactions between pairs of proteins belonging to a common protein complex, based on high-quality protein complex databases and curated co-complex association maps (Figure 1C).
evidence: Statistical enrichment analysis with reference to figure

claim: Co-abundance edges showed significant enrichment for interactions between pairs of proteins belonging to a common protein complex.
source: Co-abundance edges showed significant enrichment for (i) shared Gene Ontology (GO) terms, (ii) the literature curated PPI network used throughout this study, and (iii) interactions between pairs of proteins belonging to a common protein complex, based on high-quality protein complex databases and curated co-complex association maps (Figure 1C).
evidence: Statistical enrichment analysis with reference to figure

claim: The average shortest distances between co-abundance network nodes and known CVD drug targets are shorter for the combined network than the PPI network only.
source: We found that, for both M(IFNγ) and M(IL-4), the average shortest distances between the co-abundance network's nodes and known CVD drug targets from the integrated Complex Traits Network (iCTNet) database (Wang et al., 2015) (see Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) are shorter for the combined network than the PPI network only (Figure 1D).
evidence: Network distance analysis with reference to figures

claim: The addition of co-abundance edges resulted in an average shortest distance distribution that is shifted significantly towards lower values compared to the addition of randomly chosen edges.
source: Proving that this effect cannot be attributed to the mere addition of edges, the addition of co-abundance edges resulted in an average shortest distance distribution that is shifted significantly towards lower values compared to the addition of the same number of randomly chosen edges (Figure 1D).
evidence: Statistical comparison with randomized control

claim: The area under the ROC curve (AUROC) was significantly increased with the addition of co-abundance links compared to the PPI network only.
source: Compared to the PPI network only, the area under the ROC curve (AUROC) was significantly increased with the addition of co-abundance links (p=0.018, p=0.003 and p=0.015 for M(-), M(IFNγ) and M(IL-4), respectively, paired t-test following k-fold cross-validation) (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Statistical analysis of prediction performance with reference to figures

claim: Known CVD drug targets were more predominantly ranked in higher quantiles in the three co-abundance enriched networks compared to the PPI network only.
source: The distribution of known CVD drug targets ordered by prediction rank indeed showed that they were more predominantly ranked in higher quantiles in the three co-abundance enriched networks compared to the PPI network only (Figure 2C).
evidence: Analysis of ranking distributions with reference to figure

claim: Co-abundance networks contribute to the increase in prediction performance significantly more than random edge addition.
source: We found that co-abundance networks contribute to the increase in prediction performance significantly more (empirical p-value<0.05) than the random case (Figure 2D).
evidence: Statistical comparison with randomized control

claim: The top-ranked proteins showed significant enrichment in inflammation, innate immune response, and coronary artery disease signatures.
source: The top prioritized (empirical p-value<0.01, see Materials and methods) were significantly enriched in all three datasets for both stimulations (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Enrichment analysis with reference to supplementary file

claim: The majority of the enriched pathways of the top prioritized proteins were common across conditions.
source: The majority of the enriched pathways of the top prioritized proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1) were common (Figure 3A).
evidence: Pathway enrichment analysis with reference to figures

claim: M(IFNγ) is enriched in pro-inflammatory pathways such as p38 MAPK and NF-κB activation related pathways.
source: Focusing on the condition-specific pathways, we found that M(IFNγ) is enriched in pro-inflammatory pathways such as p38 MAPK and NF-κB activation related pathways, as well as pathways related to PI3K-Akt activation, NFAT and hypertrophy of the heart, adrenergic signaling in cardiomyocytes and interleukin signaling
evidence: Pathway enrichment analysis

claim: M(IL-4) is enriched in Rho GTPase activation, SUMOylation, β-catenin, scavenger receptor and Fas (CD95) signaling related pathways.
source: whereas M(IL-4) is enriched in Rho GTPase activation, SUMOylation, β-catenin, scavenger receptor and Fas (CD95) signaling related pathways (Figure 3B, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for full list).
evidence: Pathway enrichment analysis with reference to figures

claim: The top five final candidates for M(IFNγ) ranking were GBP1, WARS, TGM2, NAMPT and STAT1.
source: The top five final candidates for the M(IFNγ) ranking were GBP1, WARS, TGM2, NAMPT and STAT1, excluding PARP14, which was among the iCTNet drug targets.
evidence: Results of combined ranking analysis

claim: STAT1 belongs to a family of molecules known to be expressed in the heart.
source: STAT1 belongs to a family of molecules known to be expressed in the heart (Xuan et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: STAT1 plays a role in the link between coronary artery disease and inflammatory responses in vascular cells.
source: STAT1 belongs to a family of molecules known to be expressed in the heart (Xuan et al., 2001), and to play a role in the link between coronary artery disease and inflammatory responses in vascular cells (O'Donnell and Nabel, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: GBP1 and WARS showed the most dramatic changes with IFNγ stimulation in protein abundance and gene expression.
source: Of these candidates, GBP1 and WARS showed the most dramatic changes with IFNγ stimulation in protein abundance and gene expression alike (Figure 4D).
evidence: Analysis of expression data with reference to figure

claim: The top five final candidates for M(IL-4) were LIPA, TGM2, EVL, PFKP and LRRFIP1.
source: On the other hand, the top five final candidates for M(IL-4) were LIPA, TGM2, EVL, PFKP and LRRFIP1
evidence: Results of combined ranking analysis

claim: Evidence had linked WARS with vascular angiogenesis and homeostasis.
source: Evidence had linked WARS with vascular angiogenesis and homeostasis (Ewalt and Schimmel, 2002; Otani et al., 2002; Wakasugi et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Genome-wide linkage studies have previously implicated WARS in myocardial infarction.
source: Further, genome-wide linkage studies have previously implicated this molecule in myocardial infarction (Broeckel et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Subsequent genetic-epidemiological studies did not find significant associations between WARS and the risk of myocardial infarction.
source: although subsequent genetic-epidemiological studies did not find significant associations between WARS and the risk of myocardial infarction (Zee et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Secretion of the full-length form of WARS is induced by pro-inflammatory stimuli, including bacterial-derived lipopolysaccharides (LPS).
source: A more recent study that used human primary peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) demonstrated that secretion of the full-length form of WARS is induced by pro-inflammatory stimuli, including bacterial-derived lipopolysaccharides (LPS), suggesting a role for WARS in the defense system against infection (Ahn et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Silencing of WARS enhanced the mRNA expression of the chemokine CCL2 in THP-1 cells stimulated by IFNγ.
source: In THP-1 cells stimulated by IFNγ, silencing of WARS enhanced the mRNA expression of the chemokine CCL2, and the secretion of its protein (Figure 5A)
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: Silencing of WARS enhanced the secretion of CCL2 protein in THP-1 cells stimulated by IFNγ.
source: In THP-1 cells stimulated by IFNγ, silencing of WARS enhanced the mRNA expression of the chemokine CCL2, and the secretion of its protein (Figure 5A)
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: Silencing of WARS had no effect on TNFα expression in THP-1 cells stimulated by IFNγ.
source: however no such effects were observed for the cytokine TNFα (Figure 5A).
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: The enhanced secretion of CCL2 in response to WARS silencing was confirmed in three different PBMC donors.
source: The enhanced secretion of CCL2 in response to WARS silencing was confirmed in three different PBMC donors, where the increase in CCL2 secretion was significant at 12 hr of IFNγ stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental validation in primary cells with reference to figure

claim: The transcriptional levels of STAT1 and JAK2 did not change with WARS silencing.
source: Investigating the effect of WARS on the JAK-STAT pathway, the transcriptional levels of STAT1 and JAK2 did not change with WARS silencing (Figure 5A).
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: Silencing of WARS increased the phosphorylation of STAT1 at Ser701 in THP-1-differentiated macrophage-like cells.
source: Silencing of WARS, however, increased the phosphorylation of STAT1 at Ser701 in both THP-1-differentiated macrophage-like cells and human primary macrophages (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figures

claim: Silencing of WARS increased the phosphorylation of STAT1 at Ser701 in human primary macrophages.
source: Silencing of WARS, however, increased the phosphorylation of STAT1 at Ser701 in both THP-1-differentiated macrophage-like cells and human primary macrophages (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figures

claim: GBP1 is a member of the IFNγ-inducible GBP family.
source: GBP1 is a member of the IFNγ-inducible GBP family, whose members are protective against bacterial (Kim et al., 2011) and parasite (Selleck et al., 2013) infection.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: GBP family members are protective against bacterial infection.
source: GBP1 is a member of the IFNγ-inducible GBP family, whose members are protective against bacterial (Kim et al., 2011) and parasite (Selleck et al., 2013) infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: GBP family members are protective against parasite infection.
source: GBP1 is a member of the IFNγ-inducible GBP family, whose members are protective against bacterial (Kim et al., 2011) and parasite (Selleck et al., 2013) infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: GBP3 and GBP6 expression levels increase during foam cell formation in mice following a Western-type diet.
source: Following a Western-type diet GBP3 and GBP6 expression levels increase during foam cell formation in mice, indirectly suggesting their role in the acceleration of atherosclerosis by hypercholesterolemia (Goo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: GBP1 silencing resulted in a significant decrease in CCL2 secretion in human PBMC-derived macrophages stimulated with IFNγ.
source: In human PBMC-derived macrophages from four different donors stimulated with IFNγ, GBP1 silencing resulted in a significant decrease in CCL2 secretion without change to its mRNA at 24 hr of IFNγ treatment (Figure 5C).
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: GBP1 silencing did not change CCL2 mRNA levels in human PBMC-derived macrophages stimulated with IFNγ at 24 hr.
source: In human PBMC-derived macrophages from four different donors stimulated with IFNγ, GBP1 silencing resulted in a significant decrease in CCL2 secretion without change to its mRNA at 24 hr of IFNγ treatment (Figure 5C).
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: GBP1 silencing did not change the expression of TNFα and JAK2 in human PBMC-derived macrophages stimulated with IFNγ.
source: The expression of TNFα and JAK2 did not change (Figure 5C).
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: NSC756093 interrupts the interaction between GBP1 and proto-oncogene serine/threonine-protein kinase (PIM1).
source: To assess the effect of currently available therapeutic inhibitors targeting GBP1, we used NSC756093 that interrupts the interaction between GBP1 and proto-oncogene serine/threonine-protein kinase (PIM1), the inhibition of which could potentially revert paclitaxel resistance in cancer cells (Andreoli et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: NSC756093 treatment resulted in a dose-dependent decrease in the secretion of CCL2 in human primary macrophages stimulated with IFNγ.
source: Human primary macrophages were pretreated with NSCT56093 (10 to 100 nM) and then stimulated with IFNγ for 24 hr. We observed a dose-dependent decrease in the secretion of both CCL2 and TNFα (Figure 5D)
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: NSC756093 treatment resulted in a dose-dependent decrease in the secretion of TNFα in human primary macrophages stimulated with IFNγ.
source: Human primary macrophages were pretreated with NSCT56093 (10 to 100 nM) and then stimulated with IFNγ for 24 hr. We observed a dose-dependent decrease in the secretion of both CCL2 and TNFα (Figure 5D)
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: NSC756093 treatment did not change the mRNA levels of CCL2, TNFα, JAK2 and GBP1 in human primary macrophages stimulated with IFNγ.
source: with no change to their mRNA levels and to the mRNA levels of JAK2 and GBP1 itself (Figure 5D).
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: Silencing of GBP1 decreased the expression of JAK2 at 6 hr of IFNγ stimulation in THP-1 macrophage-like cells.
source: Silencing of GBP1 decreased the expression of JAK2 and phospho-STAT1 at 6 hr of IFNγ stimulation in THP-1 macrophage-like cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: Silencing of GBP1 decreased the expression of phospho-STAT1 at 6 hr of IFNγ stimulation in THP-1 macrophage-like cells.
source: Silencing of GBP1 decreased the expression of JAK2 and phospho-STAT1 at 6 hr of IFNγ stimulation in THP-1 macrophage-like cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental results with reference to figure

claim: The top five candidates of pro-inflammatory macrophage activation all contained binding sites suitable for small molecules.
source: The top five candidates of pro-inflammatory macrophage activation all contained binding sites suitable for small molecules, with at least 50% tractable structures and 20% druggable structures (see Materials and methods, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: In silico druggability analysis with reference to figure

claim: WARS and GBP1 were the two candidates with the highest percentage of druggable structures among the top five candidates.
source: Among these, WARS and GBP1 were the two candidates with the highest percentage of druggable structures (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: In silico druggability analysis with reference to figure

claim: The literature-based PPI network contained 170,303 interactions between 14,213 proteins after removal of duplicated edges.
source: After the removal of duplicated edges, the resulting PPI network contained 170,303 interactions between 14,213 proteins.
evidence: Description of network construction methodology

claim: The largest connected component (LCC) of the PPI network has 170,253 interactions and 14,115 proteins.
source: For our analyses, we discarded the isolated nodes that only self-interact and used the largest connected component (LCC) of this network, which has 170,253 interactions and 14,115 proteins.
evidence: Description of network used in analysis

claim: The PPI network has an average degree of 24.12.
source: The resulting network has an average degree <k > of 24.12, an average clustering coefficient <C> of 0.210, a diameter of 12 and an average shortest path length of 3.54 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Network topology measurements

claim: The PPI network has an average clustering coefficient of 0.210.
source: The resulting network has an average degree <k > of 24.12, an average clustering coefficient <C> of 0.210, a diameter of 12 and an average shortest path length of 3.54 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Network topology measurements

claim: The PPI network has a diameter of 12.
source: The resulting network has an average degree <k > of 24.12, an average clustering coefficient <C> of 0.210, a diameter of 12 and an average shortest path length of 3.54 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Network topology measurements

claim: The PPI network has an average shortest path length of 3.54.
source: The resulting network has an average degree <k > of 24.12, an average clustering coefficient <C> of 0.210, a diameter of 12 and an average shortest path length of 3.54 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Network topology measurements

claim: THP-1 cells were originally generated from the peripheral blood monocytes from 1 year-old male infant with acute monocytic leukemia.
source: THP-1 cells were originally generated from the peripheral blood monocytes from 1 year-old male infant with acute moncytic leukemia.
evidence: Description of cell line origin

claim: THP-1 cells were differentiated into macrophage-like cells by stimulation with 200 ng/mL of PMA for 48 hr.
source: THP-1 cells were plated in 12-well plates at 1.0 × 106 per well and differentiated into macrophage-like cells by stimulation with 200 ng/mL of PMA (Sigma-Aldrich P8139) for 48 hr.
evidence: Description of experimental protocol
